▸ "Now, let's look at how we support this workload today."
• S3: system of record, durable, cost effective at this scale
• LMDB: efficient key-value random access to samples, matched our schedule well
• But LMDB relies on memory-mapped files: needs POSIX and fast, low-latency access
• So FSx for Lustre: we stage datasets from S3 onto FSx for LMDB
★ "And for a long time, that worked well."
→ "But as we scaled, that extra layer started becoming a problem."

The detour has a price

Every run

runs that need a new filesystem never start, for lack of capacity
Hours of staging

~5× cost

▸ "That extra layer has real costs."
• Every run needs fresh FSx capacity, and hours of staging before the first step
• About 1 in 4 runs that need new capacity fail to start
• Even when it works, we spend hours just staging
• Nearly 5x the regular spend goes to filesystem overhead
★ "All to copy data that already lives in S3."
The goal
Take out the filesystem. Train directly from S3, with no loss in performance.
▸ "Looking at these problems, the obvious question was: why not train directly from S3?"
• FSx is built for high throughput and low latency; S3 is object storage, a different access model
• So naturally, we were skeptical: it might run, but without a significant performance hit?
★ "There's no point in saving on storage if we pay more in compute."
→ "So the goal became: train from S3 without sacrificing training performance."

Incompatible

The mount could not provide the mmap behavior LMDB needs.
• We kept LMDB and tried Mountpoint for S3
• It looked easy
• But LMDB needs memory mapping, and Mountpoint doesn't support that
★ "So we couldn't just swap the filesystem. We had to rethink the format."

• The GPU trains on one batch while workers fetch and prepare the next ones
• We keep a queue, like a buffer: ideally another batch is always ready

04
Fixing data loading
Closing the gap
▸ "At this point, we knew two things."
• We could train from S3, but we were still 2.8x slower
• And now we knew why: the GPUs were waiting on data
★ "So the question became: how do we keep those GPUs busy?"
• Instead of making S3 behave like Lustre, we rethought the data loader
• Two opportunities: how we read data from S3, and how we processed it afterwards
→ "Fixing those made all the difference. Let's start with the first."

Problem 1: the reads

One training step

For every batch, the loader reads n samples, transforms each one, collates them and hands the batch over. Batches arrived far slower than the GPU could use them.

Problem

Each sample was downloaded from S3 only when it was needed, so every read waited on S3.

Fix

Stream samples from S3 into memory ahead of time, following our pre-generated schedule, with many reads in flight across workers.

▸ "First we looked at how we read from S3."
• We already know exactly which samples we need ahead of time
• But we weren't really using that
★ "We waited for each request, and those little latencies added up."

Problem

Each sample was downloaded from S3 only when it was needed, so every read waited on S3.

Fix

Stream samples from S3 into memory ahead of time, following our pre-generated schedule, with many reads in flight across workers.

▸ "But what if we didn't have to wait?"
• What if we could look ahead, and start reading before the GPU asked for it?
• We introduced streaming reads, so the data was already on its way
• We used our predetermined schedule to prefetch upcoming samples, ahead of need
★ "Hiding S3 latency instead of waiting on it."

Problem 2: the transform

Problem

The transform expected the old record format, so every sample was converted element by element and rebuilt into it, just to be parsed again.

Fix

Arrow buffers mem-copied straight into tensors. No per-element conversion, no rebuilding the old record format.

▸ "Prefetching helped, but we were still chewing on samples too late."

Engineering challenges & lessons learned

01 · Multiprocessing
Fork safety with Lance + Rust
Problem

Loader workers hung.

Cause

Forking after Lance initialized Rust runtime threads.

Fix

Use forkserver; initialize Lance inside each worker.

02 · Memory
Metadata cache pressure
Problem

Host memory was exhausted.

Cause

Multiple dataset handles added metadata-cache overhead.

Fix

Share a session and cap the metadata cache.

03 · Distributed writes
S3 503 SlowDown
Problem

High-concurrency writes were throttled.

Cause

Many parallel writers targeting one S3 prefix.

Fix

Larger upload parts; exponential-backoff retries.

▸ "So we've eliminated the filesystem, gotten rid of the operational overhead, and done all of this without sacrificing performance."
• "But getting here wasn't entirely straightforward. We ran into a few interesting engineering challenges along the way."
[CLICK]
• 1. Multiprocessing: Python forks after Lance starts its Rust threads; the threads don't survive, workers hang. Fix: forkserver, initialize Lance inside the worker
• 2. Memory: multiple dataset handles, each with its own metadata cache, exhausted host memory. Fix: share a session, cap the cache
• 3. Writes: many parallel writers on one S3 prefix hit 503 SlowDown during dataset generation. Fix: larger upload parts, exponential backoff
[PAUSE]
• "Three very different problems: multiprocessing, memory management, and distributed writes."
★ "Changing your storage architecture isn't just about picking a new format."
→ "You also have to understand how that format interacts with the rest of your infrastructure."

• S3: each read takes longer, but with many requests in flight and prefetching, we hide that latency
• As long as the loader keeps up with GPU demand, the extra latency doesn't touch training performance
